A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FaceXFormer and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices. Corresponding methods and experiments can be reliably matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original facial-analysis benchmark results, component and backbone ablations, cross-dataset evaluations and qualitative predictions.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds face-recognition evaluations, an attention ablation and computational comparisons.

M1.justification: Sections 3.3–3.4 extend the existing framework with a PartialFC face-recognition head and an ArcFace loss term in joint training. The encoder, MLP fusion, task-token interactions and two-layer decoder remain unchanged; the newly emphasized bidirectional attention already existed in v2.

E1.justification: v3 adds identity verification, using MS1MV3 for training and LFW, CFP-FP, AgeDB, CALFW and CPLFW for evaluation. This introduces identity, age-gap and pose-gap verification requirements beyond the retained facial-analysis tasks, including LFWA attribute/gender testing. FFHQ and MORPH-II already appear in both appendices.

E2.justification: The new recognition comparison in Table 6 includes CosFace, ArcFace, VPL-ArcFace and AdaFace, alongside existing comparators SwinFace and Faceptor. Table 9 also introduces a computational comparison with Faceptor. Comparator membership in the retained original-task benchmarks is unchanged; QFace has no recognition scores.

E3.justification: v3 adds verification accuracy, aligned recognition inputs without augmentation, an attention control and FP16/FP32 computational evaluation. Table 7 redescribes v2's 'without FXDec' control as retaining self-attention but removing cross-attention, while retaining its scores; whether it was rerun is unspecified. The bias table's reported training-data count changes from 400K to 5.9M.

E4.justification: The component ablation gains a standard-cross-attention control that directly tests bidirectional attention's contribution. v3 also adds component-level computational analysis and revises qualitative cases to emphasize occlusions, extreme poses and accessories. The backbone ablation is retained in Appendix C, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates for its experiments.

E6.justification: New Table 6 reports mean recognition accuracy of 95.94% for FaceXFormer, alongside 95.28% for Faceptor and 97.22% for SwinFace. Tables 7 and 9 add attention-control and computational results, including 100.1 FP16 FPS. Original-task benchmark, backbone and cross-dataset scores are retained numerically despite expanded reported training coverage. Qualitative predictions also change.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 extends the mathematical definition of the joint objective with a weighted ArcFace recognition-loss term. The fusion and attention equations otherwise match, and neither version introduces theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions expand the central claim from nine to ten simultaneous facial-analysis tasks, adding recognition while retaining the 33.21 FPS claim. The introduction also introduces a specific claim of a 69.44% speed advantage over previous multi-task models.

C2.justification: v3 attributes recognition shortcomings to conflicting identity-related training objectives and links efficiency more explicitly to bidirectional attention. It removes v2's limitations concerning complete retraining, interactivity and promptability, and removes the appendix caveat about inconsistent age and race predictions. These qualifications were not merely relocated.

D1.justification: Appendix F.7 adds recognition dataset characteristics, sample and identity counts, five-keypoint alignment and the absence of augmentation. Section 3.1 newly reports 983K MLP-fusion parameters. Existing hardware, optimizer, training schedule, batch size, other task preprocessing and project access information are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Table 2 substantially expand architectural positioning against QFace and Faceptor through fusion mechanisms, decoder depth, pretraining and computational cost. Recognition literature and Query2Label are added, while RepFormer and FDN references are removed. The comparison shifts beyond the earlier emphasis on task coverage.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experimental discussion and conclusion are extensively revised around recognition and efficiency. Component ablations move into the main text, while backbone analysis and broader-impact discussion move into the appendix. The main Discussion section disappears and appendix sections are reorganized.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned and moved to the first page; Figure 2 gains a recognition branch. Figure 3 expands from three to five displayed examples, and appendix qualitative panels change. Three new comparison tables, a redesigned component-ablation table with corrected metric labels, and relocated backbone results substantially alter the visual organization.

improvement.justification: The new attention control and computational breakdown in Tables 7 and 9 provide more direct evidence for central design and efficiency claims, while Table 6 evaluates the recognition extension. These gains are tempered by removal of useful retraining/promptability limitations and age/race failure disclosures. The new 69.44% speedup claim also does not match the tabulated FPS comparison. Overall, the stronger empirical support provides a limited net improvement.
